_meta.notes: Comprehensive index for Cambodia covering prehistoric settlements, Funan maritime kingdom, Chenla, Khmer Empire (Angkor Wat, Jayavarman VII), post-Angkor decline, Vietnamese/Thai pressure, French protectorate 1863, Sihanouk era, secret US bombing, Khmer Rouge genocide (1975-1979), Vietnamese invasion, UNTAC, Hun Sen era, and modern reconstruction.

country_profile.government_type: Unitary parliamentary constitutional monarchy (de facto dominant-party)

religion.note: Buddhism is state religion; Khmer Rouge tried to destroy religion 1975-1979; Islam practised by Cham minority

ethnic_groups.name: Khmer
ethnic_groups.notes: Austro-Asiatic (Mon-Khmer); dominant in all aspects; Angkorian heritage; Khmer script derived from Indian Brahmi; rice-paddy wet cultivation

ethnic_groups.name: Cham
ethnic_groups.notes: Austronesian; Muslim; descended from Champa kingdom (Vietnam); settled along Mekong; targeted by Khmer Rouge genocide; fishing communities

ethnic_groups.name: Chinese
ethnic_groups.notes: Teochew/Cantonese/Hokkien; historically commercial class; Phnom Penh business community; targeted by Khmer Rouge; intermarriage with Khmer

ethnic_groups.name: Vietnamese
ethnic_groups.notes: Mekong fishing communities; historically marginalised; periodic expulsions; Tonlé Sap floating villages

ethnic_groups.name: Indigenous (Khmer Loeu/Highland Khmer)
ethnic_groups.notes: Austroasiatic (Mnong, Stieng, Jarai, Tampuan, Kreung, Brao, Kuy); northeastern highlands (Ratanakiri, Mondulkiri); animist traditions; swidden agriculture; 24 recognised groups

ethnic_groups.name: Thai/Lao
ethnic_groups.notes: Border areas; Khmer-Thai intermixing; Kuy people straddle Cambodia-Thailand border

country_profile.notes_unique: Angkor Wat is world's largest religious monument; Khmer Rouge killed ~1.7-2.5 million (25% of population); Tonlé Sap is largest freshwater lake in SE Asia; Cambodian flag is only national flag depicting a building

geography.terrain: Mostly flat low-lying plains (Central Lowland); Tonle Sap basin; Cardamom Mountains in southwest; Dangrek Range along Thai border
geography.notes: Tonle Sap is SE Asia's largest freshwater lake (expands 5x during monsoon); Mekong River critical; rapid deforestation (lost 25%+ forest since 2000).

economy_extended.notes: Garment/footwear exports dominant; tourism (Angkor Wat); construction boom (Chinese investment); highly dollarized economy (80% USD); EBA trade preferences; Sihanoukville transformed by Chinese investment; deforestation for plantations.

health.notes: Remarkable HIV/AIDS decline (from 1.7% to 0.5%); Khmer Rouge destruction of medical profession (almost all doctors killed); drug-resistant malaria epicentre; road traffic deaths among highest in region.

food_agriculture.notes: World's largest producer of Kampot pepper (GI protected); rice exporter; Tonle Sap largest inland fishery in the world; freshwater fish protein source critical; land concessions controversial (displacement of communities).

energy.notes: Imports 50%+ electricity from Vietnam, Thailand, Laos; Lower Sesan II dam controversial (Chinese-built, displaced communities, environmental damage); floating solar on reservoirs; coal power growing; first offshore oil production expected.

transport.notes: Mekong River important transport corridor; road quality improving rapidly (Chinese/Japanese investment); Siem Reap new international airport (2023); railway system rehabilitated (Phnom Penh-Sihanoukville); tuk-tuks ubiquitous.

tourism.notes: Angkor Wat world's largest religious monument; tourism ~15% of GDP; dark tourism (Khmer Rouge sites); Sihanoukville transformed by Chinese casinos; backpacker trail popular; Preah Vihear temple border dispute with Thailand.

legal_system.notes: 1993 constitution; de facto one-party state under CPP/Hun family since 1985; Extraordinary Chambers in Courts of Cambodia (Khmer Rouge tribunal); judiciary lacks independence; CNRP opposition dissolved 2017.

human_rights_gender.notes: Authoritarian governance; opposition suppressed; NGOs increasingly restricted; land displacement widespread; garment worker exploitation despite reforms; trafficking concerns; relatively tolerant toward LGBTQ+ culturally.

security_stability.notes: World's most heavily mined country per capita; CMAC mine clearance ongoing (64,000+ casualties since 1979); political stability under authoritarian control; Ream Naval Base expansion (suspected Chinese military use); border disputes with Thailand/Vietnam.

cultural_heritage.notes: Khmer Empire (9th-15th c.) one of history's greatest civilisations; Angkor Wat largest religious monument globally; Khmer Rouge (1975-79) destroyed 90% of intellectuals/artists; cultural revival ongoing.

comparative_rankings.notes: Rapid economic growth but poor governance and environmental scores; Angkor Wat massive soft power asset; mine contamination legacy.
comparative_rankings._note: Country position relative to continent and global. 'rank' = 1 is best/largest.

current_leader.name: Hun Manet
current_leader.title: Prime Minister
current_leader.notes: CPP; son of Hun Sen; West Point graduate; hereditary succession in all but name; king is Norodom Sihamoni

king.name: Norodom Sihamoni
king.title: King
king.notes: Ceremonial; former ballet dancer and UNESCO ambassador; son of Sihanouk; unmarried; apolitical

former_leaders.name: Norodom Sihanouk
former_leaders.notes: 'Father of independence'; abdicated 1955 to be PM (Sangkum); overthrown by Lon Nol 1970; allied with Khmer Rouge; restored as king 1993; abdicated 2004; died 2012

former_leaders.name: Lon Nol
former_leaders.notes: Khmer Republic; US-backed; overthrown by Khmer Rouge April 17, 1975

former_leaders.name: Pol Pot (Saloth Sar)
former_leaders.notes: Khmer Rouge; 'Brother Number One'; directed genocide; Year Zero; emptied cities; S-21/Tuol Sleng; died 1998

former_leaders.name: Hun Sen
former_leaders.notes: CPP; world's longest-serving PM (38 years); former Khmer Rouge defector; strongman; dissolved opposition (CNRP) 2017; handed power to son Hun Manet 2023

910.name: Prehistoric Cambodia and Funan
910.description: Early human settlement in the Mekong basin, the emergence of the Indianized maritime kingdom of Funan as one of Southeast Asia's earliest states, and its role as a conduit of Indian culture.

sub_clusters.name: Prehistoric Mekong Settlements
sub_clusters.description: Archaeological sites revealing early habitation in the Mekong delta and Tonle Sap region, the development of rice cultivation, and early bronze and iron age communities.

sub_clusters.name: Kingdom of Funan
sub_clusters.description: The rise of Funan as a major maritime trading state, its port of Oc Eo, Indian cultural and religious influences, diplomatic missions to China, and its gradual absorption by Chenla.
key_events: Foundation legend of Funan — the Brahmin Kaundinya marries Queen Soma (1st century AD)
Funan sends embassies to the Chinese court and dominates maritime trade routes (3rd–5th centuries)

910.name: Chenla Kingdom
910.description: The successor state to Funan, the split into Land Chenla and Water Chenla, the period of political fragmentation, and the foundations of Khmer political culture that would lead to Angkor.

sub_clusters.name: Rise and Split of Chenla
sub_clusters.description: Bhavavarman I's conquest of Funan, the consolidation of Chenla as an inland power, the division into Land Chenla and Water Chenla, Javanese raids, and the political chaos preceding Jayavarman II.
key_events: Isanavarman I establishes Isanapura (Sambor Prei Kuk) as Chenla's capital (early 7th century)

920.name: Angkor Empire Foundation and Classical Period
920.description: Jayavarman II's declaration of independence and the founding of the Khmer Empire, the construction of the great temple-mountains, Angkor Wat, and the zenith of Khmer civilization.

sub_clusters.name: Jayavarman II and Empire Founding
sub_clusters.description: Jayavarman II's declaration as chakravartin on Mount Kulen in 802 AD, the establishment of the devaraja cult, and the early Angkorian kings who built the first temple complexes.
key_events: Jayavarman II declares independence from Java and founds the Khmer Empire on Phnom Kulen (802 AD)

sub_clusters.name: Angkor Wat and Suryavarman II
sub_clusters.description: The construction of major temple complexes culminating in Angkor Wat under Suryavarman II, military campaigns against Champa and Dai Viet, and the apogee of classical Khmer art and architecture.
key_events: Suryavarman II begins construction of Angkor Wat, the world's largest religious monument (c. 1113–1150)

sub_clusters.name: Cham Invasion and Crisis
sub_clusters.description: The period of political instability after Suryavarman II, the devastating Cham naval invasion and sack of Angkor in 1177, and the empire's near-collapse before Jayavarman VII's counterattack.
key_events: Champa launches a naval invasion up the Tonle Sap and sacks Angkor (1177)

920.name: Jayavarman VII and Angkorian Zenith
920.description: The reign of Jayavarman VII, the shift to Mahayana Buddhism, the construction of Angkor Thom and the Bayon, the overextension of the empire, and the gradual decline leading to Angkor's abandonment.

sub_clusters.name: Jayavarman VII's Buddhist Empire
sub_clusters.description: Jayavarman VII's defeat of Champa, his conversion of the state religion to Mahayana Buddhism, the construction of Angkor Thom, the Bayon, Ta Prohm, and an enormous road and hospital network.
key_events: Jayavarman VII defeats Champa and builds Angkor Thom with the Bayon as its center (c. 1190–1210)
Construction of 102 hospitals and extensive road network across the empire

sub_clusters.name: Theravada Shift and Decline of Angkor
sub_clusters.description: The gradual conversion to Theravada Buddhism, the rise of the Thai kingdoms of Sukhothai and Ayutthaya, repeated Thai invasions, the loss of western provinces, and the final abandonment of Angkor.
key_events: Thai armies from Ayutthaya sack Angkor, leading to its abandonment as the capital (1431)

930.name: Post-Angkorian and Middle Period
930.description: The relocation of the capital to the Phnom Penh area, the transformation into a Theravada Buddhist maritime state, and the continuing struggle against Thai and Vietnamese encroachment.

sub_clusters.name: Longvek Kingdom
sub_clusters.description: The establishment of new capitals at Phnom Penh, Lovek, and Longvek, the flourishing of Theravada Buddhism, engagement with Portuguese and Spanish traders, and the fall of Longvek to Siam.
key_events: Portuguese and Spanish missionaries and traders arrive in Cambodia (1550s–1580s)
Siamese forces capture and sack Longvek (1594)

930.name: Dark Age and Vietnamese-Thai Domination
930.description: Cambodia's 'Dark Ages' — caught between expansionist Siam and Vietnam, progressive loss of the Mekong Delta to Vietnamese settlers, and the near-extinction of Cambodian sovereignty.

sub_clusters.name: Siamese and Vietnamese Interference
sub_clusters.description: Rival Thai and Vietnamese factions installing puppet kings, the loss of Prey Nokor (Saigon) and the Mekong Delta to Vietnam, and Cambodia's reduction to a buffer state.

sub_clusters.name: Vietnamese Occupation and Siamese Wars
sub_clusters.description: The Vietnamese attempt to annex Cambodia outright and impose cultural assimilation, the Cambodian rebellion, the Siamese-Vietnamese War fought on Cambodian soil, and the appeal to France for protection.
key_events: Vietnam imposes direct rule on Cambodia and attempts cultural Vietnamization (1835–1840)
King Norodom seeks French protection to escape Thai-Vietnamese domination (1863)

940.name: French Colonial Period
940.description: The French Protectorate, colonial exploitation, the rediscovery and restoration of Angkor, the rise of Cambodian nationalism, and the Japanese wartime interlude.

sub_clusters.name: French Protectorate and Angkor Rediscovery
sub_clusters.description: The establishment of the French Protectorate, Henri Mouhot's popularization of Angkor in the West, the EFEO's archaeological restoration work, colonial economic transformation, and early nationalist stirrings.
key_events: Henri Mouhot's published accounts bring Angkor to Western attention (1860s)
French impose a convention stripping the king of most remaining powers (1884)

sub_clusters.name: WWII, Japanese Occupation and Independence
sub_clusters.description: Vichy French and Japanese joint control, the brief Japanese-sponsored independence of 1945, Son Ngoc Thanh's nationalism, King Sihanouk's 'Royal Crusade for Independence', and the Geneva Accords.
key_events: King Norodom Sihanouk achieves full independence through his 'Royal Crusade' (9 November 1953)

950.name: Sihanouk Era and Khmer Republic
950.description: Sihanouk's Sangkum Reastr Niyum and neutralist balancing act, the Vietnam War's spillover, the Lon Nol coup, the Khmer Republic, and the devastating US bombing campaign.

sub_clusters.name: Sangkum Reastr Niyum
sub_clusters.description: Sihanouk's abdication to become head of state, the Sangkum political movement, Cambodian neutrality during the Cold War, the secret Ho Chi Minh Trail operations, and growing internal opposition.
key_events: Sihanouk abdicates and creates the Sangkum Reastr Niyum movement (1955)

sub_clusters.name: Lon Nol Coup and Khmer Republic
sub_clusters.description: The US-backed Lon Nol coup, the proclamation of the Khmer Republic, Sihanouk's alliance with the Khmer Rouge, the massive US bombing campaign (Operation Menu/Freedom Deal), and the republic's collapse.
key_events: Lon Nol overthrows Sihanouk in a US-backed coup (18 March 1970)
US conducts intensive carpet bombing of Cambodia (1970–1973)

950.name: Khmer Rouge Genocide
950.description: The Khmer Rouge's radical agrarian revolution under Pol Pot, the evacuation of cities, the killing fields, the deaths of an estimated 1.5–2 million people, and the Vietnamese invasion that ended the regime.

sub_clusters.name: Democratic Kampuchea
sub_clusters.description: The Khmer Rouge's 'Year Zero' ideology, forced evacuations of cities, abolition of money, religion, and private property, the Tuol Sleng (S-21) prison, mass executions, and famine under the Pol Pot regime.
key_events: Khmer Rouge captures Phnom Penh and begins forced evacuation of the entire city (17 April 1975)
An estimated 1.5–2 million Cambodians die from execution, starvation, and disease (1975–1979)

sub_clusters.name: Vietnamese Invasion and Regime Fall
sub_clusters.description: Khmer Rouge border attacks on Vietnam, the Vietnamese full-scale invasion, the fall of Phnom Penh, and the establishment of the People's Republic of Kampuchea.
key_events: Vietnam invades Cambodia and topples the Khmer Rouge regime (January 1979)

960.name: Peace Process and UNTAC
960.description: The Vietnamese-backed PRK government, the Cambodian civil war, the 1991 Paris Peace Accords, the UNTAC peacekeeping mission, and the restoration of the monarchy under Sihanouk.

sub_clusters.name: PRK and Civil War
sub_clusters.description: The People's Republic of Kampuchea under Vietnamese protection, the Coalition Government of Democratic Kampuchea resistance, the Thai border refugee camps, and the Cold War geopolitics preventing resolution.

sub_clusters.name: Paris Peace Accords and UNTAC
sub_clusters.description: The 1991 Paris Peace Accords, the UNTAC-supervised elections of 1993, the restoration of the monarchy, the fragile coalition government, and Hun Sen's 1997 coup against FUNCINPEC.
key_events: Paris Peace Accords signed, ending the Cambodian conflict (23 October 1991)
UNTAC-supervised elections restore democratic governance (May 1993)

960.name: Modern Cambodia and Hun Sen Era
960.description: Hun Sen's consolidation of power, rapid economic growth, the Khmer Rouge tribunal (ECCC), democratic backsliding, the transfer of power to Hun Manet, and Cambodia's role in ASEAN.

sub_clusters.name: Hun Sen Consolidation and Economic Growth
sub_clusters.description: Hun Sen's dominance of Cambodian politics, garment industry and tourism-driven economic growth, the ECCC war crimes tribunal, the death of King Sihanouk, and Chinese investment.
key_events: Extraordinary Chambers in the Courts of Cambodia (ECCC) begins Khmer Rouge trials (2006)
Former King Norodom Sihanouk dies in Beijing (15 October 2012)

sub_clusters.name: Democratic Backsliding and Power Transfer
sub_clusters.description: The dissolution of the CNRP opposition party, the suppression of press freedom, the controversial 2018 and 2023 elections, and the transfer of the prime ministership to Hun Sen's son Hun Manet in 2023.
key_events: Supreme Court dissolves the Cambodia National Rescue Party (CNRP) (November 2017)
Hun Sen transfers power to his son Hun Manet as Prime Minister (August 2023)

unassigned_events.note: Events not yet assigned to a thematic cluster
